correctness.rationale: Positivity forces both integer exponents ≤t=N−1, and this condition is sufficient even on the diagonal where equal powers carry to one bit. There are ts labeled pairs. A two-bit value determines its unordered exponent positions uniquely, and a second labeling is available exactly when both distinct positions are r-th powers. One-bit values do not collide with two-bit values or with each other, so subtracting binom(s,2) gives the exact count for all allowed cutoffs, including t=1. Algebra gives Z=−{t^(1/r)}−s(s−1)/(2t); the extra term is a shift by −1/2 plus O(t^(−1/2)) for r=2 and O_r(t^(−1/r)) for r≥3. In a full block [k^r,(k+1)^r), count the corresponding integer interval [(k+α)^r,(k+β)^r); relative to its uniform target the error is O_r(k^(r−2)+1), uniformly in endpoints. The sum of these errors is O_r(K^(1−1/r)), and the single unfinished block is of that order at most. On a dyadic index block of size T, a threshold comparison can change only in a fractional-root interval of length O_r(T^(−1/r)); the difference of two prefix bounds gives O_r(T^(1−1/r)) exceptional indices. Summing these bounds proves the uniform-in-threshold rate and the shifts stated. Boundedness of Z gives an O(N) error, and its nondegenerate limiting law rules out convergence to any constant and hence a constant linear correction with o(N) remainder.
residual_risks: No uniformity in r, optimal Kolmogorov rate, or corresponding real-cutoff law is asserted. The bundled finite enumeration concerns only the exact count and multiplicity.

value.rationale: The value is identifying the exact size and distribution of the leading asymptotic's fluctuations in a natural subfamily of the general Romanoff set, not the routine binary-encoding argument alone. The square case has a different secondary law because collisions survive at linear scale; higher powers have no such shift. The nondegenerate law settles the natural question of whether a deterministic second coefficient exists at dyadic cutoffs.
residual_risks: This does not address the prime-plus-set representation problem or arbitrary real cutoffs.
